# Flight!

- Energetically expensive per unit time (= burn lots of calories each minute)
- Energetically efficient per unit distance (= go farther for each calorie)

# Flight aerodynamics: Bernoulli lift

$$
P_{static} + P_{dynamic} = P_{total}
$$
$$
\rho * A * V = C
$$

(where $P$ is pressure, $\rho$ is density, $A$ is area, $V$ is velocity, and $C$ is a constant---increase the area above a wing with constant air density, and velocity must increase, reducing static pressure and generating **lift**)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/airfoil.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([MIT](https://web.mit.edu/16.00/www/aec/flight.html))

# Which combination will increase Bernoulli lift?

$$
P_{static} + P_{dynamic} = P_{total}
$$
$$
\rho * A * V = C
$$

a) larger wings and constant speed
b) smaller wings and constant speed
c) greater speed and larger wings
d) a & c
e) impossible to say


# Flight aerodynamics: Newtonian lift

("equal and opposite reaction": air is deflected downward when there is a positive angle of attack)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/newton.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Bajec & Heppner 2009)  

# Flight aerodynamics: lift from vortices

(spirals of air off a leading bird's wing can provide lift to a follower)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/vortices.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Bajec & Heppner 2009)  

# Ibises exploit lift from vortices!

(most flaps occur in theoretically optimal position)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/ibis_flight.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Portugal et al. 2014)  

# Drag

- **induced drag**: drag from air streams deflecting from wing---reduced by alula!
- **parasitic drag**: friction between bird and air 
- **profile drag**: related to form of wing


\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/alula.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Portugal et al. 2014)  

# Flght energetics

- Upper left: high power needed to overcome weight
- Upper right: high power needed to overcome drag
- $V_{MP}$: speed with minimum energy use per unit time
- $V_{MR}$: speed for maximum distance per unit energy

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/energetics.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)  

# Flapping generates lift and thrust

- **Flight stroke** consists of **upstoke** and **downstoke**
- rotating wing forward generates forward thrust, rotating back minimizes drag ("flap, fold, and twist")
- from 2x / second (Gray Heron) to $\sim$ 80x / second (hummingbirds) 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/flapping}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Shyy et al. 2013)

# Thermal soaring

- Thermal soarers exploit rising hot air columns, gliding from one to another
- Examples: vultures, frigatebirds

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/thermal.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Goto et al. 2022)

# Dynamic soaring

- Dynamic soarers exploit deflected wind, turning into currents to rise and and away to glide forward
- Examples: pelagic seabirds, hawks along mountains

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/dynamic.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Goto et al. 2022)

# Hummingbird hovering

- Figure-8 motion
- Up to 78 cyles (upstrokes + downstrokes) per second!

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/hummers.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gJ_T_Y1rxHw

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)

# Flight ecomorphology

- Wing aspect ratio=$\frac{\text{Wingspan}}{\text{Wing area}}$
- Wing loading=$\frac{\text{Body mass}}{\text{Wing area}}$

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/aspect.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019) 

# Which species would you expect to have the lowest wing aspect ratio?  

a) a frugivorous parrot
b) a pelagic seabird
c) a hummingbird
d) a grouse 
e) a migratory songbird

# Major wing muscles and furcula

- **pectoralis** powers the downstroke
- **supracoracoideus** operates as pulley through triosseal canal (gap between scapular, coracoid, furcula) to power upstroke
- **furcula**: expands and contracts with wing beats; may enhance respiratory performance

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/supracoracoideus.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird_anatomy))
